passage: Javier tripped on the playground gravel and sat there, lip trembling, knees stinging, tears starting. Rafael, who had been rolling a red toy truck along the wall, stopped. He walked over, looked at Javier's face, and pushed the truck across the gravel to him. When Javier kept crying, Rafael put an arm halfway around his shoulders and patted twice; Javier leaned toward him. Their teacher, Ms Ortiz, crouched nearby. “Rafael, you gave Javier your truck. You saw he was sad and wanted to help.” Rafael nodded and looked at the truck.

qa.q: What toy did Rafael push across the gravel to Javier?
qa.a: He pushed a red toy truck across the gravel.

qa.q: What did Rafael want when he pushed the truck over and patted Javier?
qa.a: He wanted to make Javier feel better; he saw the sad face and gave something he liked. It is a simple offer, and he may also have just wanted the crying to stop.

qa.q: How could Ms Ortiz's words help Rafael learn?
qa.a: By naming that he saw Javier was sad and wanted to help, she links the feeling to the caring act. She could also ask Javier what he would like.

qa.q: How might Javier feel about the truck and the pat?
qa.a: He may feel comforted that someone noticed, though his knees still sting and a truck may not be what he wanted. Leaning toward Rafael is the clue that the closeness was welcome. 🤍

grounding: Early sympathy: a child offers a toy and a pat to a crying friend, and an adult names it.

passage: During free play at the community centre creche, Darshan started crying loudly when his mother waved goodbye at the door and left for work. Urmila, at the block table, stared at him. She picked up her stuffed elephant and held it out. “This is Bholu. He can sit with you.” Darshan pushed it away, still crying. Urmila frowned, then sat down beside him without a word and kept Bholu on her own lap, patting his head. Caregiver Sunita noticed. “Urmila, you stayed with him. That is kind.”

qa.q: What did Urmila offer Darshan?
qa.a: She offered her stuffed elephant, Bholu.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when Darshan pushed the elephant away, and what else might it mean?
qa.a: Probably confused or a little disappointed but still wanting to comfort him, since she sat down beside him. It could also be that she was unsure what to do and staying was easiest.

qa.q: How could Sunita build on this moment?
qa.a: She could keep naming what Urmila did, and gently tell her that Darshan may want quiet company more than a toy right now.

qa.q: What is it like for Darshan when the toy is offered?
qa.a: He is missing his mother, so an elephant may not fix it, and pushing it away does not mean he disliked Urmila's offer. Her quiet sitting beside him may feel safer.

grounding: A young child offers a toy and stays near a crying friend; the adult names it.

passage: The children call me Sudha Aunty. I was hanging washing when the boy downstairs started crying; his kite had torn on the gate. Parul, from the next flat, stopped skipping. She watched him a moment, then trotted over and hugged him hard around the middle, rope still in her hand. He kept crying. She pulled back, frowned, and held out her skipping rope instead. I can't know what went on in that small head. But when her mother came down, she said, “Parul, you saw he was sad and wanted him to feel better. That's caring.” Parul nodded seriously.

qa.q: What had happened to the boy's kite?
qa.a: His kite had torn on the gate.

qa.q: Why did Parul hold out her skipping rope after the hug?
qa.a: She seems to have felt concerned and wanted him to stop being sad, so when the hug didn't work she tried a gift; she may also have felt unsure what else to do.

qa.q: How did Parul's mother help her learn from this moment?
qa.a: She named what Parul had noticed and done, linking the boy's sadness to Parul's caring, which helps Parul understand her own kindness.

qa.q: How does Sudha see what Parul was thinking?
qa.a: Sudha only sees the actions and admits she cannot know Parul's thoughts, but the hug and the rope look to her like simple, real care.

grounding: Shows a young child offering a hug and then a toy to a crying child, and an adult naming the feeling behind it.

passage: Monday: Mahima cried at the preschool gate when her papa left. Baljeet stood by the shoe rack, staring, thumb in mouth. Tuesday: Mahima cried again. Baljeet walked over, pushed his toy tractor into her hands and said, “Vroom.” She sniffed and held it. The teacher crouched beside them. “Baljeet, you saw Mahima was sad, so you shared. That's kind.” Baljeet grinned. Thursday: A new boy wailed by the door. Baljeet looked at Mahima. Together they carried the tractor over, and Baljeet patted the boy's arm. “Sad. Here.”

qa.q: What toy did Baljeet give Mahima?
qa.a: Baljeet pushed his toy tractor into her hands.

qa.q: What might Baljeet have been feeling as he stared on Monday?
qa.a: He was probably puzzled and a little worried by her crying, though he might just have been shy or curious in the new place.

qa.q: How did the teacher's words on Tuesday help Baljeet?
qa.a: By saying that he saw Mahima was sad and shared, the teacher linked her feeling to his kind act, so he could use it again on Thursday.

qa.q: What was the tractor like for Mahima on Tuesday?
qa.a: It gave her something to hold and showed that someone had noticed her, so she sniffed and calmed a little instead of crying alone.

grounding: Shows a young child's simple sympathy, a shared toy and a pat, growing after an adult names the link between feelings and care.

passage: The band was so loud at the wedding that nobody heard Jyoti cry. She had pinched her finger in a folding chair and sat under the table, sobbing. Hemant, crawling after a balloon, found her. He looked at her finger, then at her face. He wrapped both arms round her, awkward and tight, then pushed his half-eaten laddoo into her good hand. When that didn't help, he ran out and tugged his Masi's sari until she bent down. Masi scooped Jyoti up and said to him, “You saw she was hurting and you brought help. That was caring, Hemant.”

qa.q: Where did Hemant find Jyoti?
qa.a: Hemant found her under the table, sobbing.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when he looked at her finger and then her face?
qa.a: He likely felt worried and sorry for her, which shows in his tight hug and the laddoo; he may also have felt a bit helpless when neither worked.

qa.q: Which of Hemant's choices helped most, and why?
qa.a: Fetching his Masi helped most, because in the loud hall an adult could look after the pinched finger when a hug and a sweet could not.

qa.q: What would change if the band had been quiet?
qa.a: An adult might have heard Jyoti straight away, and Hemant would not have had to find her and bring help himself.

grounding: Shows a young child offering a hug and a sweet to a crying child in a noisy place, and an adult naming the act as caring.

passage:
In the colony park, Saurabh's balloon slipped from his fingers and floated up over the water tank. Saurabh sat on the slide and cried.

Shankar stopped digging. He watched for a moment, then walked over, sat very close and held out his red toy car. "You can drive it first."

Saurabh kept crying, but he took the car.

Shankar's grandmother called softly from the bench, "Shankar, you saw your friend was sad and you shared. That's kindness." Shankar patted Saurabh's back, twice, like a grown-up.

qa.q: What did Shankar hold out to Saurabh?
qa.a: His red toy car.

qa.q: What might Shankar have been feeling as he watched Saurabh cry?
qa.a: He was probably sad for his friend and concerned, wanting to make things better. He may also have been unsure what to do at first, since he watched before moving.

qa.q: How did Shankar's grandmother help him link feelings and care?
qa.a: She named what he did, noticing his friend was sad and sharing, so he learns that kindness is an answer to someone's sadness.

qa.q: How might Saurabh experience Shankar sitting so close?
qa.a: Saurabh is still upset about the balloon, but a friend nearby with a toy may make him feel less alone.

grounding: It shows a young child offering a toy and closeness to a crying friend, and an adult naming it so he links feelings with care.
